title: Every Order ID, Once
description:
`source_orders` is the live production system; `warehouse_orders` is what landed in the analytics warehouse after the last sync. They're supposed to agree, but don't always.

Report every distinct `order_id` that appears in **either** system, with no duplicates even if an id appears in both.

Name the column `order_id`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: source_orders has ids 1, 2, 3, 4 and warehouse_orders has ids 1, 2, 5. Combined without duplicates, the result is 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
hint: Plain UNION already removes duplicates across the two SELECTs — you don't need DISTINCT on top of it.

title: Present In Both Systems
description:
Report every `order_id` that appears in **both** `source_orders` and `warehouse_orders`.

Name the column `order_id`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: Only order ids 1 and 2 appear in both systems. Orders 3 and 4 are source-only and order 5 is warehouse-only.
hint: INTERSECT keeps only rows present in both SELECTs — exactly "in both systems".

title: Orders That Never Synced
description:
Report every `order_id` that exists in `source_orders` but is **missing** from `warehouse_orders` — orders that failed to sync.

Name the column `order_id`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: Orders 3 and 4 exist in the source system but never made it to the warehouse. Orders 1 and 2 are in both systems and are excluded.
hint: EXCEPT is one-directional: `A EXCEPT B` means "in A, remove anything also in B". Order of the two SELECTs matters here.

title: Out Of Sync, Either Direction
description:
Report every `order_id` that is out of sync between `source_orders` and `warehouse_orders` **in either direction** — present in one system but not the other.

Name the column `order_id`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: Orders 3 and 4 are source-only, and order 5 is warehouse-only. Together they form the three out-of-sync ids. Orders 1 and 2 are in both systems and are not reported.
hint: This is a symmetric difference: one EXCEPT for each direction, combined with UNION. Careful — chained set operators evaluate left-to-right at equal precedence in SQLite, not "EXCEPT before UNION". `A EXCEPT B UNION C EXCEPT D` means `((A EXCEPT B) UNION C) EXCEPT D`, not two independent EXCEPTs joined by UNION. SQLite won't let you parenthesize compound-select operands directly either — wrap each EXCEPT as its own subquery in FROM instead.

title: Count Out-Of-Sync Orders By Direction
description:
Report how many orders are out of sync **in each direction** between `source_orders` and `warehouse_orders`: how many exist only in source, and how many exist only in the warehouse.

Name the columns `direction` (`source_only` or `warehouse_only`) and `n`. Return exactly two rows, in any order.
outputExplanation: Two orders (3, 4) are source-only and one order (5) is warehouse-only.
hint: Use UNION ALL here, not UNION — you want exactly one row per direction even if both counts happen to be equal (UNION would collapse them into one row).

title: Orders That Fully Agree
description:
An order only "fully agrees" between systems if **both** its `order_id` and its `amount` match. Report every `(order_id, amount)` pair that appears in both `source_orders` and `warehouse_orders` exactly as-is.

Name the columns `order_id` and `amount`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: Order 1 ($120) and order 2 ($80) have identical id and amount in both systems. Orders 3 and 4 don't exist in the warehouse at all.
hint: INTERSECT compares whole rows (every selected column together), not just the first one — an order_id match with a different amount will not survive here.

title: Build An Audit Log Of Both Systems
description:
Build a combined audit log listing every row from `source_orders` and every row from `warehouse_orders`, tagged with which system it came from. Unlike the reconciliation queries above, **duplicate rows must be preserved** here — if source has the same order twice, the log should show it twice.

Name the columns `order_id`, `customer_name`, `amount` and `system` (`source` or `warehouse`). Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: The audit log contains all 4 source rows (tagged 'source') and all 3 warehouse rows (tagged 'warehouse'), for 7 rows total. Orders 1 and 2 appear twice — once from each system.
hint: This is exactly the case UNION ALL exists for — an audit log should never silently drop a real duplicate row the way UNION would.

title: Three-Way Reconciliation
description:
There are now **three** systems: `source_orders`, `warehouse_orders` and `vendor_orders`. For every `order_id` that appears in at least one of them, report how many of the three systems contain it.

Name the columns `order_id` and `system_count`. Return the result in any order.
solutionSql:
SELECT order_id, COUNT(*) AS system_count
FROM (
  SELECT DISTINCT order_id FROM source_orders
  UNION ALL
  SELECT DISTINCT order_id FROM warehouse_orders
  UNION ALL
  SELECT DISTINCT order_id FROM vendor_orders
)
GROUP BY order_id;
outputExplanation: Order 1 appears in all three systems (count=3). Orders 2 and 3 appear in two systems each. Orders 4, 5 and 6 appear in only one system each.
hint: DISTINCT the order_ids from each system *before* combining them with UNION ALL — otherwise a duplicate row inside one system's own table would inflate its count, when it should only ever count as "present" once per system.

title: Match Customers Despite Messy Formatting
description:
The same customer is recorded with inconsistent formatting across systems — `'Ann Lee'` in one, `'ANN LEE'` or `'  ann lee '` in another. Report every customer name (normalized to lowercase with no leading/trailing whitespace) that appears in **both** `source_orders` and `warehouse_orders`, once formatting differences are accounted for.

Name the column `customer`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: After normalizing names to lowercase with trimmed whitespace, 'ann lee' and 'ben kim' appear in both systems. A hidden test shows that without normalization, '  ben kim ' and 'BEN KIM' would be missed as matches.
hint: Normalize both sides the same way (LOWER + TRIM) before comparing — INTERSECT on the raw customer_name column would miss matches that are really the same person.

title: Reconcile Despite Duplicate-Row Noise
description:
A sync bug sometimes inserts the same order into `source_orders` twice. That duplication is not a real discrepancy and must not be reported as one. Report every `order_id` that is genuinely out of sync between `source_orders` and `vendor_orders` — present in one but not the other — regardless of how many times a row happens to be duplicated on either side.

Name the column `order_id`. Return the result in any order.
outputExplanation: Orders 2 and 4 are source-only, and order 6 is vendor-only. Orders 1 and 3 appear in both and are excluded. A hidden test duplicates order 1 inside source_orders to confirm the query isn't fooled by row duplication.
hint: A row-count comparison ("source has 5 rows, vendor has 4") would be fooled by the duplicate. EXCEPT and UNION both operate on distinct sets, so a plain symmetric difference is naturally immune to duplicate noise — no extra DISTINCT needed. Just wrap each EXCEPT as its own subquery in FROM, since chained set operators are otherwise evaluated left-to-right rather than nesting the way you'd expect.
